answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 19 No. 6 (text of 24.10.1980, never amended) guarantees freedom of conscience, belief and worship to 'todas las personas'. Ley 19.638 (published 14.10.1999) was also in force: under Art. 6, freedom of religion means 'para toda persona' the right to profess, practise and change religion. No practice evidence from around 2000 was read; the rating is carried back from the 2004 State Department report, so it is low confidence.

Same provisions as in 2000, unchanged. The State Department's 2004 Chile report says the government 'generally respected' religious freedom and that 'All denominations practiced their faiths without restriction'. It notes some unequal treatment of Protestant churches, but nothing aimed at migrants.

Same provisions as before. Ley 20.050 (2005) amended other parts of Art. 19 but not No. 6. The State Department's 2009 report says the constitution provides for freedom of religion and the government generally respected it. It mentions neo-Nazi violence against immigrants, which is societal abuse, not state action on religion.

Same provisions as before. Ley 20.609 (24.07.2012) added a civil anti-discrimination action that covers 'la religión o creencia' and 'la nacionalidad'. The State Department's 2014 report records no restrictions on religious freedom. No migrant-specific breach was found.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 rating 'Rarely; Sometimes' has no documented practice behind it. No source found shows the state restricting migrants' religious freedom, and the MRD itself rated 2023 'Usually'. The apparent drop from 2015 to 2020 more likely reflects a different coder than a real change in practice.
answers.notes: The protection rests on the Constitution ('asegura a todas las personas') and Ley 19.638 Art. 6 ('para toda persona'). No treaty or court ruling was relied on. DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 1 (exclusion or expulsion of those who propagate doctrines aimed at violent change) does not concern religion.

answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 19 No. 12 (freedom 'de emitir opinión ... sin censura previa') applied to all persons. So did Ley 16.643 Art. 1 (1991–2001 version), which said the right 'que garantiza a todos los habitantes ... incluye el de no ser perseguido a causa de sus opiniones'. DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 1/Art. 17 allowed foreigners to be excluded or expelled as 'agitadores o activistas' of violent doctrines; this targets acts and propaganda, not holding an opinion. No practice evidence from around 2000; the rating is extrapolated.

Ley 19.733 (in force 04.06.2001) replaced Ley 16.643. Its Art. 1 keeps 'no ser perseguido ni discriminado a causa de las propias opiniones' for 'todas las personas'. Ley 19.742 (25.08.2001) amended the last paragraph of Art. 19 No. 12 (film rating replaced censorship), which does not touch holding opinions. The 2004 State Department report says freedom of speech was generally respected.

No change to the provisions. The 2009 State Department report says freedom of speech was generally respected, with criticism of laws against insulting state institutions. Nothing in it is specific to migrants.

No change to the provisions; Ley 20.609 (2012) added 'ideología u opinión política' as a ground of arbitrary discrimination. The 2014 State Department report says speech was generally respected. In 2017 (after this date) foreigners were expelled for 'anarchist' views and 'antisystemic activities' and courts annulled the orders. That points to gaps toward the 2020 period.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: The Constitution's notes and the 1991–2001 version of Ley 16.643 were read on LeyChile. Practice evidence is general State Department reporting, plus 2017 press reports on expulsions of foreigners for their views. Nothing was read for around 2000.
answers.notes: The Yes rests on the Constitution and Ley 16.643/19.733 Art. 1, which cover all persons. DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 1 is a foreigner-specific ground for exclusion or expulsion tied to propagating violent doctrines. The 2017 expulsions show it was used against foreigners for their beliefs, with the courts correcting it.

answers_by_date.basis: The starting 'No' is kept: nothing between 2000 and 2020 changed the position. On 1 January 2000 the restrictions specific to foreigners were tighter than later. Ley 16.643 Art. 5 required owners of newspapers and concessionaires of radio and TV to be Chilean, and directors were also subject to a nationality requirement. DL 1.094 Arts. 15 No. 1 and 17 allowed expulsion of those who 'propaguen o fomenten de palabra o por escrito' doctrines aimed at violent change.

Ley 19.733 (04.06.2001) replaced Ley 16.643. Art. 1 guarantees expression to 'todas las personas', but Arts. 9–10 still require media legal representatives and directors to be 'chilenos', which narrowed but kept the nationality requirement. DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 1 was unchanged. Ley 19.742 (2001) replaced film censorship with a rating system for everyone.
No relevant change: Ley 19.733 Arts. 9–10 and DL 1.094 Arts. 15 No. 1 and 17 still applied.

No relevant change. Ley 20.507 (08.04.2011) amended only DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 2 (smuggling and trafficking), not No. 1. Ley 20.609 (2012) added an anti-discrimination action but did not remove the restrictions on foreigners.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.sourcing_note: The pre-2001 Ley 16.643 version, Ley 19.733 and DL 1.094 were read in their LeyChile versions. The answer stays No throughout, so implementation does not apply.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 'No' does not fit the 'Yes' given for opinion (q83) and religion (q81), which cite the same provisions (Art. 19 No. 12 and Ley 21.325 Art. 13). Constitution Art. 19 No. 12 and Ley 19.733 Art. 1 guarantee expression to 'todas las personas'. The 'No' is defensible only through the restrictions specific to foreigners: nationality requirements for media directors and representatives (Ley 19.733 Arts. 9–10) and the expulsion ground in DL 1.094 Arts. 15 No. 1 and 17. But the nationality requirements still exist under Ley 21.325 and the MRD codes 2023 'Yes', so the 2020 'No' may be a coding inconsistency.
answers.notes: No court ruling stating a general rule was relied on. The 2017 expulsion annulments are practice evidence, read in a press report only.

answers_by_date.basis: The starting 'No' (no equal protection for irregular migrants) is kept; no event between 2000 and 2020 changed it. In 2000: Constitution Art. 19 No. 15 (association) and No. 19 (unionisation 'en los casos y forma que señale la ley'); Labour Code Art. 212 (private-sector workers may form unions). Old Labour Code Art. 236 had no nationality requirement for union directors. DL 1.094 Arts. 15 No. 1 and 17 allowed expulsion of foreigners 'sindicados' as agitators.

Ley 19.759 (in force 01.12.2001) replaced Labour Code Art. 236 so that union-director requirements are set by each union's statutes. Neither the old nor the new text has a nationality condition, so the change does not bear on migrants. The other provisions were unchanged.
Ley 20.414 (04.01.2010) amended Art. 19 No. 15 on political-party primaries only. No change for migrants.

Ley 20.500 (16.02.2011), Art. 1: 'Todas las personas tienen derecho a asociarse libremente'. This applies to non-profit associations, not unions, and does not address irregular migrants' union membership. Ley 20.609 (2012) covers discrimination based on 'sindicación'. The basis of the starting 'No' is unchanged.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: I looked for a union or association protection for migrants between 2000 and 2020 that was later repealed or narrowed. I read the Labour Code Arts. 212–216 and 236 with their notes, Ley 19.759 No. 45, the pre-2001 Art. 236 as quoted by the Dirección del Trabajo, the earlier union decree-law (idNorma 6991), Constitution Art. 19 Nos. 15 and 19 with their notes, Ley 20.500 and DL 1.094 Arts. 15 and 17. Nothing was found that was narrowed in that period. The only nationality condition on union leaders (the decree-law's Art. 21, 'Ser chileno') predates 2000, and the 2000 text of Art. 236 had none.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'No' rests on the claim that irregular migrants 'cannot join trade unions'. No provision read says so: Labour Code Art. 212 grants the right to 'los trabajadores' without any status condition, and Art. 236 has no nationality requirement. The barrier, if any, is practical (no work authorisation or formal contract) or comes from DL 1.094's expulsion grounds, not an express statutory exclusion. The starting answer may be too strict, but it is kept.
answers.notes: Implementation does not apply because the answer is No throughout. No court ruling was relied on.

answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 19 No. 13 (unchanged since 1980) guarantees all persons the right 'a reunirse pacíficamente sin permiso previo y sin armas'. Meetings in public places are subject to general police rules. DL 1.094 Arts. 15 No. 1 and 17 allowed expulsion of foreign 'agitadores o activistas'. No practice evidence from around 2000; the rating is extrapolated from 2004.
No change to the provisions. The 2004 State Department report says freedom of assembly was 'generally respected'. It is not specific to migrants.
No change to the provisions. The 2009 State Department report says assembly was generally respected. No migrant-specific restriction is documented.

No change to the provisions. The 2014 State Department report says assembly was generally respected. The drop in the 2020 rating follows later practice: the 2017 expulsions of foreigners for 'antisystemic activities', which courts annulled, and the late-2019 government policy of expelling foreigners arrested during the social unrest.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: LeyChile's notes show Art. 19 No. 13 was never amended. Practice evidence for 2005–2015 is general State Department reporting, not specific to migrants, and there is none for around 2000. The 2017 and 2019 items are press reports.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 rating 'Effectively Never; Sometimes' is not one of the instrument's options, since the two levels are not neighbours. The 2019 expulsions mostly concerned irregular migrants arrested for looting rather than for peaceful assembly. 'Sometimes' alone would fit the evidence better.
answers.notes: The protection rests on Constitution Art. 19 No. 13 ('asegura a todas las personas'). Implementation before 2015 is inferred from general reports that do not single out migrants.

answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 19 No. 2 only bars 'diferencias arbitrarias'. Art. 19 No. 16 expressly lets the law require Chilean nationality in employment. DL 1.094 had no non-discrimination clause, and no statute named migrant status as a protected ground.
No change. Ley 20.050 (26.08.2005, after this date) amended Art. 19 Nos. 4 and 16 on matters unrelated to migrants and kept the nationality clause in No. 16.
No change to the relevant provisions.

Ley 20.609 (24.07.2012) prohibits arbitrary discrimination on grounds including 'la nacionalidad', but not migratory status. The starting answer reads this as falling short of a ban on discrimination for being a migrant, and no later event changes that before 2020.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

provisions.instrument: Ley 20.609, establece medidas contra la discriminación

events.what_changed: Amended the professional-associations paragraph of No. 16. The clause allowing the law to require Chilean nationality was left untouched, and the amendment does not bear on migrants.
events.passage: Se prohíbe cualquiera discriminación que no se base en la capacidad o idoneidad personal, sin perjuicio de que la ley pueda exigir la nacionalidad chilena o límites de edad para determinados casos.

events.what_changed: A general ban on arbitrary discrimination with a court remedy. Its grounds include nationality, race and ethnicity, but not migratory status.
events.passage: se entiende por discriminación arbitraria toda distinción, exclusión o restricción que carezca de justificación razonable, efectuada por agentes del Estado o particulares ... en particular cuando se funden en motivos tales como la raza o etnia, la nacionalidad, la situación socioeconómica, el idioma

events.what_changed: Requires the state to protect foreigners' human rights 'sin importar su condición migratoria' and to promote protection against discrimination. This explains the MRD's change from 'No' in 2020 to 'Yes' in 2023.
events.passage: Artículo 3.- Promoción, respeto y garantía de derechos. El Estado deberá proteger y respetar los derechos humanos de las personas extranjeras que se encuentren en Chile, sin importar su condición migratoria, incluidos los afectos a la ley Nº 20.430.

answers.repealed_search: I looked for a ban on discrimination based on migrant status between 2000 and 2020 that was later repealed. I read the notes on Constitution Art. 19 Nos. 2 and 16 (Ley 19.611 of 1999 and Ley 20.050 of 2005), DL 1.094 (Arts. 1–17 and 62–64, the latter on grounds for rejecting permits) and Ley 20.609. No such protection was found to have existed and been repealed.

answers.sourcing_note: The constitutional notes and Ley 20.609 were read on LeyChile. Implementation does not apply. The 2014 State Department report (citing the INDH's 2013 report) documents de facto discrimination against Latin American immigrants in health and education.
answers.starting_answer_concern: There is a borderline point. From 24.07.2012, Ley 20.609 Art. 2 bans arbitrary discrimination by state agents and private parties based on 'la nacionalidad', which arguably reaches discrimination against foreigners as such. A coder could read 2015 and 2020 as 'Yes'. Migratory status is not a listed ground, though, and the list is illustrative ('tales como'), so the starting 'No' is defensible.
answers.notes: No ruling was relied on. If Ley 20.609 were read as covering migrant status, the answer would change from 2012-07-24 onward (2015 'Yes'); I did not make that change because the starting answer is kept.
